title: Max your 401(k) — employee + employer side
summary: For S-corp owner-employees: $24,500 employee deferral plus 25% employer match on W-2 wages.
detailsHtml:
S-corp owner-employee specifics

Employer contributions to a 401(k) are calculated on W-2 wages, not on distributions. This creates a tension: low salary minimizes SE/payroll tax, but limits retirement contributions. A salary level that maximizes total after-tax wealth is typically higher than the minimum reasonable salary, when retirement contribution capacity is factored in.

The §401(a)(17) compensation cap: Only the first $360,000 of W-2 wages (for 2026, indexed annually) can be considered when calculating employer plan contributions. So a $500K-salary owner can't generate more employer contribution than a $360K-salary owner — the cap binds. This affects the salary-vs-distribution optimization for very high-income S-corp owners differently than at lower compensation levels.
§415(c) is a per-employer limit, but §402(g) is aggregate: If you have W-2 income with a 401(k) and also Solo 401(k) income from an unrelated business, the §415(c) $72,000 cap applies separately to each plan — you can theoretically fill both. However, your employee deferral under §402(g) ($24,500 in 2026) is aggregate across all plans. The classic mistake is W-2 employees with side-business Solo 401(k)s deferring $24,500 in each plan, then having to remove the excess. The employer side of each plan is independent; the employee side is not.
2026 limits, age < 50: Employee deferral: $24,500 Employer (25% of $98,000 salary): $24,500 Plus mega backdoor space (up to total $72K cap) Total Roth/Traditional capacity: up to $72,000 in 2026
